content:
Seeing clearly helps you judge steps, kerbs and obstacles. When arthritis already makes moving harder, poor vision adds to falls risk.

This guide explains how vision and hearing affect falls and what can help. It is educational information, not a diagnosis or personal treatment plan.

How vision affects falls

  • Blurred vision or cataracts make hazards harder to see.
  • Bifocal or varifocal glasses can make steps hard to judge.
  • Changes in light can be hard to adjust to.
  • Reduced side vision can make you miss obstacles.

Practical steps

  • Have regular eye tests. They are free on the NHS for people aged 60 and over.
  • Keep glasses clean and well-fitting.
  • Consider single-vision glasses for walking outside.
  • Improve lighting, including night lights.
  • Mark step edges with contrasting colours.

Hearing and balance

Hearing loss is linked to a higher risk of falls, and inner ear problems can affect balance. Ask your GP about a hearing test if you are having difficulty hearing, and seek advice about dizziness.

Getting help

NICE recommends that falls assessments include checking vision. Ask your GP about a falls assessment if you have fallen or feel unsteady.

When to get help

  • Call 999 if you have sudden loss of vision, a drooping face, arm weakness or slurred speech.
  • Get urgent help from NHS 111 or an eye service for sudden eye pain, flashes, new floaters or a shadow in your vision.

Never stop or change a prescribed medicine yourself. Ask your GP or pharmacist for a review.

Common questions

How often should I have an eye test?

Usually every two years, or as your optometrist advises.

Can cataract surgery reduce falls?

Treating cataracts can improve vision. Ask your optometrist or GP.
